name: Conway's Game of Life
description: Conway's Game of Life with a grid that grows dynamically to avoid edge effects, step + timed-auto playback, and a jump-to-generation control — plus two showcase modes: Game of Life as a Turing machine (AND/OR/NOT logic gates) and Game of Life playing Game of Life (the self-simulating metapixel). Three coders compete; the team refines it across two iterations.
spec:
Build Conway's Game of Life with these properties:
1. The field must resize dynamically to avoid edge effects — as a configuration approaches the border, the grid grows (and the cells shrink accordingly).
2. It must be as visually striking as possible — use the most impressive Game-of-Life visualizations.
3. Support both step-by-step and automatic playback with adjustable speed.
4. Provide a "jump to generation N" control that shows the position after N steps.
(Original specification authored in Russian.)

narration_chapters.title: Specification — your conversation with CodeForge
paragraphs: You're watching a replay of a real CodeForge session at high speed. Every node you'll see is a real LLM that actually wrote or audited code. The clock pauses on each phase — read at your own pace, then hit Continue.
Every run starts here. The Specification is plain language describing what the app should do. This one (in Russian) asks for Conway's Game of Life with four hard requirements:

1) the field must grow dynamically so patterns never hit a wall — as a colony nears the edge, the grid expands and the cells shrink; 2) it must look genuinely striking; 3) both step-by-step and timed auto playback; 4) a "jump to generation N" control.
From this one paragraph, a small team of AI models will build, test and refine a working app — no human writes a line of code.

narration_chapters.title: Coding round 1 — three coders in parallel
paragraphs: Three different models each take the spec and write a complete implementation independently: Claude Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.5 Flash, and Claude Opus 4.7.

They don't see each other's work. Running diverse models in parallel is deliberate — each makes different choices about the grid data structure, the neighbour-counting kernel, and the rendering approach, which gives the team several strong candidates to choose from.
Watch the streaming text appear on each Coder node as the LLM generates — this is the actual token stream, not a progress bar.

narration_chapters.title: Testing round 1 — independent audits
paragraphs: Now two Testers — GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8 — review every Coder's version against the spec.

They check the things that matter for this app: does the B3/S23 rule update correctly? Does the grid actually grow before a pattern touches the border, or does it silently clip live cells? Is the render fast enough when the grid gets large? Does "jump to generation N" really fast-forward the simulation?
Each audit is a structured list of issues tagged critical / serious / minor — the raw material for the next iteration.

narration_chapters.title: Summarizer — one prioritized brief
paragraphs: Two testers × three coders is six audits. The Summarizer reads all of them and writes a single prioritized brief: the highest-impact fixes first, duplicates merged, contradictions resolved.
That brief is what the Coders read next — instead of six overlapping reviews, they get one clear to-do list.

narration_chapters.title: Iteration 2 — coders refine
paragraphs: The Coders take the brief and fix what the Testers flagged: keep a safety margin so the auto-expanding grid never clips a live cell, speed up the neighbour pass on big grids, and sharpen the visuals.
This is the core loop of CodeForge — generate, audit, summarize, refine — repeated until the code converges.

narration_chapters.title: Testing round 2 — did it converge?
paragraphs: The same Testers re-audit the refined versions. This time the issue count drops sharply — the edge-effect bug is gone and performance is in budget.
When the Testers stop finding critical and serious issues, the loop is done and the team moves to finalization.

narration_chapters.title: Summarizer — converged
paragraphs: Round-2 audits consolidated: only cosmetic suggestions remain. The code is ready to ship.

narration_chapters.title: Finalizer — picking the winner
paragraphs: The Finalizer (Claude Opus 4.8) compares all three final versions side by side on three axes: how completely they meet the spec, whether they run cleanly, and overall code quality.

Here it picks Coder 3 (Claude Opus 4.7) and writes a short README explaining the choice. The orchestrator then substitutes that coder's real code as the final result — the Finalizer selects, it doesn't rewrite.

narration_chapters.title: First version — try it
paragraphs: Here's the winning coder's first-iteration cut. It already plays Conway's Life with step and auto modes — basic, but it works.
Run it, then continue to see the polished final version the team converged on.

narration_chapters.title: Enhancement — an optional second pass
paragraphs: After the first version ships, CodeForge can run an optional Enhancement pass. Three specialists review the final code in parallel: Design (UX & layout), Functionality (features & correctness), and Security (safety & edge cases).

Here they propose the showcase features that make this build stand out — the AND/OR/NOT logic-gate mode (Game of Life as a Turing machine) and the self-simulating "Life plays Life" metapixel — plus guards on the grid growth and the jump-to-generation input.
The Enh. Summarizer then merges the three reviews into one curated, ranked list you could approve item by item before a fresh build round.

narration_chapters.title: Final version — the polished result
paragraphs: This is the result the team shipped: a dynamically growing grid that never hits a wall, step and timed-auto playback, and a jump-to-generation control — plus two showcase modes that go beyond the spec: Game of Life as a Turing machine (build AND/OR/NOT logic gates from gliders) and Game of Life playing Game of Life (the self-simulating metapixel).
Run it right here, or spin up your own session from this same spec and watch a fresh team build it live.

Каждый вентиль — подлинный паттерн B3/S23: пушки Госпера, планёры, поглотители. Переключатели на каждой карточке задают входы A/B. Результат стабилизируется ~700 поколений.

OTCA Metapixel

Гигантская конструкция 2048×2048, которая ведёт себя как одна клетка Жизни. Период такта — 35 328 поколений.

Поколение: 0 · Клеток: 0
Вычисление…

Три логические операции реализованы подлинными паттернами клеточного автомата (B3/S23): пушки Госпера, планёры, поглотители. Поток планёров = «1», его отсутствие = «0». Переключатели задают входы; цифра справа — результат после стабилизации. Каждая схема проходит фоновую самопроверку по таблице истинности.

«Жизнь, играющая в Жизнь» — OTCA Metapixel

В 2006 году участники форума ConwayLife.com (Brice Due) построили OTCA Metapixel — гигантскую конструкцию Жизни размером 2048×2048 клеток, которая ведёт себя как одна-единственная клетка другого, более крупного клеточного автомата.

Каждый «метапиксель» хранит своё состояние, считает живых соседей с помощью потоков планёров и переключается по правилам, которые можно настроить — в том числе по классическим B3/S23. Замостив плоскость такими метапикселями в форме планёра, получим гигантскую конструкцию, эволюционирующую как планёр — но «клетками» являются сами узоры Жизни.

Так Жизнь буквально симулирует саму себя: наглядная демонстрация вычислительной универсальности и самоподобия клеточных автоматов.

2048×2048 клеток / метапиксель период такта — 35 328 поколений B3/S23 внутри B3/S23 универсальность по Тьюрингу
⚠ Не удалось загрузить анимацию OTCA Metapixel из внешнего источника.
Открыть GIF напрямую: metapixel.gif ↗
